notes.meaning: Peter urges believers to arm their minds with the very same attitude that Jesus had when He suffered physical pain for them. Choosing to endure hardship for the sake of doing right shows a decisive break with the old life of sin. When a Christian is willing to suffer rather than disobey God, sin no longer has mastery over them.

A person who adopts this mindset stops chasing after selfish human desires during their remaining time on earth. Instead, they make God's will their everyday rule and guide. Life in this mortal body is short, so believers are called to invest their remaining days in what pleases God.

Believers have already spent far too much of their past living like their unbelieving neighbours. Peter names unrestrained passions, drunkenness, wild partying, and lawless idol worship as evils that belong strictly to the past. Remembering how much time was wasted in sin gives Christians strong reason to live differently today.

Former companions are surprised and confused when Christians refuse to plunge back into wild and wasteful behaviour with them. Because they do not understand this radical change, they insult and mock believers. A holy life convicts the consciences of the worldly, which often provokes their anger and slander.

Those who mock and mistreat God's people will one day have to answer directly to God for their words. He stands fully prepared to act as Judge over everyone, both those alive on earth and those who have already died. Persecuted Christians can rest in the knowledge that ultimate justice belongs to the Lord.

The gospel was preached to believers while they were still alive who have since faced physical death. Though human beings judged and condemned them in the body, they now live on with God in the spirit. This assured Peter's readers that physical death and martyrdom do not rob faithful Christians of their eternal reward.

differ.view: Some hold that Christ descended between His death and resurrection to proclaim the finished work of salvation to Old Testament saints resting in the realm of the dead.
Martin Luther treated this verse as exceptionally mysterious and expressed honest uncertainty about its exact meaning.

notes.meaning: Peter announces that the culmination of all history has drawn near since Christ began the last days. Because the Lord's return can happen at any time, believers must stay clear-minded, calm, and self-controlled. Keeping a sober mind guards a person from spiritual carelessness and keeps their prayer life healthy.

Above every other duty, believers must keep their love for one another deep and fervent. Genuine love willingly overlooks and forgives the faults of others rather than exposing them to cause division. When love flourishes in a church, offenses are quietly put away instead of stirring up conflict.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: An older Catholic interpretation understood this to mean that acts of charity and almsgiving can help make satisfaction for a believer's own sins.

notes.meaning: Christians are commanded to welcome others and open their homes, especially to traveling brothers and sisters in need. This hospitality must be given gladly, without secret murmuring or grumbling about the cost and trouble. Practicing hospitality with a willing heart turns ordinary meals and lodging into acts of Christian love.

Every believer has received a gift or ability through God's varied and colorful grace. Christians are not independent owners of these abilities but managers, or stewards, who must use them to serve others. Using our gifts for the good of the church honours the Master who entrusted them to us.

Anyone who speaks in the church must deliver God's truth faithfully, as someone conveying divine messages rather than personal opinions. Anyone who serves must rely on the strength God provides rather than merely their own energy. The ultimate aim in all speech and service is that God receives glory through Jesus Christ forever.

Peter calls his readers beloved friends and tells them not to be shocked by the painful persecutions testing them. Hard trials are not strange accidents or signs of God's rejection, but refining fires designed to test and purify their faith. Believers should expect hostility from an ungodly world rather than being surprised by it.

Believers should rejoice because their present trials mean they are sharing in the sufferings of Christ. Enduring hardship for His sake links them with Jesus now and guarantees boundless joy when He returns in glory. The willingness to suffer with Him today prepares the heart for the great celebration of tomorrow.

If people insult a believer because they belong to Christ, that Christian is truly blessed. The glorious Spirit of God rests upon them with special comfort and power during seasons of reproach. The world may treat them with contempt, but God honors them with His presence.

Peter warns believers never to confuse suffering for Jesus with suffering the rightful punishment for crimes. No Christian should bring trouble on themselves by committing murder, stealing, doing general wrongs, or meddling in other people's affairs. Pain that comes from bad behaviour brings shame rather than honor.

If anyone faces hardship simply because they follow Jesus, they should feel no shame at all. Instead, they ought to praise God for the honor of bearing the name Christian. Enduring mockery with patience glorifies the Savior whose name they carry.

God's refining judgment begins first with His own household, purifying the church through trials. If God disciplines His own beloved family with such seriousness, the final end awaiting those who reject the gospel will be terrible indeed. Believers can take comfort knowing that their current trials are a loving discipline, not a final condemnation.

Peter quotes the book of Proverbs to ask what will become of the ungodly if even the righteous are saved through great difficulty. Discipleship is described as hard because walking the path of faith involves fiery trials and renouncing sin, not because God's grace is deficient. Those who live in open rebellion against God will find no place to stand in the day of wrath.

Those who endure suffering according to God's wise purpose should deposit their lives safely into the hands of their faithful Creator. God has both the power and the love to keep what is entrusted to Him. Even while facing hardship, believers must keep their focus on doing good.
